q: Which of these needs is the most reasonable fit for the Singleton pattern?
options: A User object for each person who logs in
One shared settings object loaded once from a config file
Any data that two classes need to share with each other at run time
A Point(x, y) value created thousands of times per second
why: Singleton fits when the program truly needs exactly one instance with one access point, like settings read once at startup. Even then, many teams create it once and pass it in, which keeps code easy to test.
wrong: There are many users, each with their own state, so one instance is wrong by definition.
Sharing data is better done by passing objects; a singleton for this creates hidden global state.
Small value objects are meant to be created freely; one shared Point cannot hold different values.

q: Database is a Singleton. A unit test for priceWithTax() wants a fake price instead of a real database. Why is that hard, and what helps?
options: getInstance() is not thread-safe; making it synchronized lets tests replace it
Each test can call getInstance() and gets a fresh, empty Database
Make the Database constructor public so tests can create their own copy
The dependency is hidden inside the method; pass a price source in instead
why: PriceService reaches for a global, so a test cannot swap it. Passing a price source (or the Database behind an interface) into the constructor makes the dependency visible. The app can still create just one real instance and share it.
wrong: Thread safety is a separate issue; locking does not let a test swap in a fake.
getInstance() returns the same object every time, so state also leaks from one test to the next.
PriceService still calls getInstance(), so a copy the test creates is never used.

q: Two threads call Logger.getInstance() at the same moment, the first time it is used. What can happen with this code?
options: Both may see null and each create a Logger, so two instances exist
Nothing: static fields are thread-safe in Java by default
The two threads deadlock, waiting on each other inside getInstance()
The second thread gets null back, because the first is still in new
why: The null check and the assignment are separate steps. Both threads can pass the check before either one assigns, so the constructor runs twice. Common fixes are creating the instance eagerly or guarding the creation with synchronization.
wrong: Static means one per class, not thread-safe; nothing here stops two threads from interleaving.
No locks are taken, so there is nothing to wait on and no deadlock.
A thread that sees null creates and assigns its own Logger, so this method never returns null.

q: An app picks a parser from the file extension at run time: .csv gets CsvParser, .json gets JsonParser. Callers should not know the concrete classes. Which pattern fits?
options: Singleton, so the whole program shares a single parser object
Observer, so every parser is notified each time a file is opened
Factory: one place maps the extension to a Parser and returns it
Decorator, so each new parser wraps the one before it
why: The concrete type depends on data known only at run time. A factory keeps that decision, and every new, in one place and returns the common Parser type. Callers just call parse(), and adding XML changes only the factory.
wrong: Singleton controls how many instances exist, not which class to create.
Observer is about reacting to events, not about choosing and creating an object.
Decorator adds behaviour to one object by wrapping it; it does not choose between types.

q: An HttpRequest has a required URL and eight optional settings. Constructors with long parameter lists keep causing mix-ups. A teammate suggests a Factory. Which pattern fits better?
options: Factory, since any pattern that creates objects solves this
Builder: set only the options you need, by name, then build()
Singleton, so a single shared request is configured once for everyone
Adapter, so the long constructor gets a shorter interface
why: The problem is assembling one complex object with many optional parts, which is what Builder is for: named steps, defaults for the rest, and often an immutable result. A Factory answers a different question: which class to create.
wrong: Both are creational but solve different problems; a factory still needs all the values passed in.
Requests differ from call to call; sharing one would mix settings between callers.
Adapter converts one existing interface into another that a client expects; it does not help with optional arguments.

q: Checkout must price shipping as standard, express or store pickup, chosen by the user at run time, and more options are planned. Which pattern fits?
options: Strategy: one ShippingCost interface with a class per option
Observer: each option subscribes to the checkout's events
Singleton: one global shipping calculator for every option
Adapter: convert express pricing into the standard interface
why: The algorithms are interchangeable and selected at run time, which is the core of Strategy. Checkout calls cost(order) on whichever option it was given, and a new option is a new class, with no if-chain inside Checkout.
wrong: Observer notifies many listeners of an event; here the code must pick and run one calculation.
One calculator for every option brings the if-chain back inside it.
Adapter fits an existing incompatible class into an interface; nothing here needs converting.

q: A reviewer says this is not the Strategy pattern, because there is no Strategy interface or class. Is the reviewer right?
options: Yes: Strategy needs an abstract base class and one subclass per algorithm
Yes: passing a function as an argument is the Observer pattern
Yes: it is Factory, because order decides which list is created
No: show() takes an interchangeable algorithm, and a function can be one
why: Strategy is the idea of passing in an interchangeable algorithm, not a fixed class shape. In Python, and with Java lambdas, a function with the right signature is enough: by_price and by_rating are strategies that show() uses without knowing which one it got.
wrong: Classes are one way to write strategies; with first-class functions, the function is the strategy.
Observer registers listeners to be told about events; here the function only computes a sort key.
sorted() always builds a new list; order only decides how it is sorted, not what kind of object is made.

q: When a stock price changes, a chart, an alert service and a logger must all react. New reactions will be added later without editing the Stock class. Which pattern fits?
options: Strategy: Stock picks exactly one of the three reactions at run time
Factory: Stock creates the chart, alert and logger itself
Observer: listeners subscribe to Stock and get notified on change
Singleton: one global Stock that everyone polls in a loop
why: Many independent parties must react to one change, and the subject should not know who they are. Observer lets each listener register itself while Stock just loops over its subscribers. A new reaction is a new subscriber.
wrong: Strategy chooses one algorithm; here every reaction must run on each change.
If Stock creates its listeners, it must be edited for every new one, the opposite of the goal.
Polling wastes work and ties everyone to a global; Observer pushes each change instead.

q: Each time a dialog opens, it subscribes to the bus, and it never unsubscribes. After the dialog is opened and closed three times, what does publish print?
options: One line, since a new subscribe call replaces the earlier handler
Three lines, because the bus still holds all three handlers
Nothing, because the closed dialogs were garbage collected
An error, because the first two dialogs no longer exist
why: The bus's list keeps a reference to each handler, so the closed dialogs stay alive and still react. This is the classic observer leak: memory grows and stale handlers keep running. Unsubscribe when the listener is closed.
wrong: append adds to the list; nothing removes the older handlers.
An object stays in memory while something still references it, and the bus does.
The handlers are still referenced, so they exist and run without error.

q: On a price change, CacheUpdater writes the new price to a cache and PriceLabel reads the cache to redraw. It works only because CacheUpdater subscribed first. Which fix keeps the subject unaware of its listeners?
options: Add a comment that CacheUpdater must always be subscribed first
Make the cache a Singleton so both listeners use the same instance
Have the subject call CacheUpdater, then PriceLabel, directly by name
Put the new price in the event, so PriceLabel stops reading the cache
why: Observers should not rely on notification order. PriceLabel only needs the new price, so carrying it in the event removes the hidden dependency on the cache being written first. The subject still just notifies subscribers, and order no longer matters.
wrong: A comment does not stop the next change from reordering subscriptions and breaking it again.
They already share one cache; the bug is about when it is written, not how many caches exist.
It works, but the subject now knows its concrete listeners and their order, which is what the question rules out.

q: Your code expects a PaymentGateway interface with pay(amount). A vendor SDK you cannot change offers sendPayment(cents, currency). Which pattern lets your code use the SDK?
options: Adapter: a class implements PaymentGateway and calls the SDK inside
Decorator: wrap PaymentGateway so that it also gains a sendPayment method
Observer: subscribe the SDK to PaymentGateway's events
Singleton: share one SDK instance across the whole app
why: Adapter converts one interface into the one the client expects. The adapter's pay(amount) converts the amount to cents and calls sendPayment. Your code depends only on PaymentGateway, and the SDK stays untouched.
wrong: Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour; the problem here is two different interfaces.
Nothing here is an event; the code needs a call translated, not a notification.
How many SDK objects exist does not fix the mismatch between pay and sendPayment.

q: Bold and Italic each wrap another Text and add tags around its output. What does this print?
options: hi
hi
why: Each decorator calls the object it wraps, then adds its own tags. Italic is outermost, so its tags are outermost. Wrapping at run time combines features freely, instead of a subclass for every mix like BoldItalicText.
wrong: The order is reversed: the outermost wrapper, Italic, adds the outermost tags.
A decorator calls the object it wraps, so Bold's tags are kept, not replaced.
Each wrapper's render() adds its tags; nothing skips them.
